summary: This standards-track document defines an IPv6 header compression format for 6LoWPANs, updating RFC 4944. It uses shared context to compress arbitrary prefixes. It shrinks packets for tiny low-power radio networks.

plainLanguage.summary: Tiny sensors can only send small messages, so this shortens long addresses by pointing to something both sides already know.

questions: how to compress ipv6 for sensor networks
how small can an ipv6 header get on 802.15.4
subtitle: How IPv6 headers shrink to a few bytes so they fit in tiny 802.15.4 radio frames.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.15.4 links have a 127-byte MTU and about 80 octets of MAC payload with security enabled, and the compression in RFC 4944 (LOWPAN_HC1 and LOWPAN_HC2) was insufficient for most practical uses of IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: LOWPAN_IPHC squeezes the IPv6 header into 2 or 3 octets using shared context, link-layer derived addresses and short codes for common values. LOWPAN_NHC then compresses following headers, including UDP.
tldr.outcome: In the best case the IPv6 header shrinks to two octets for link-local communication, and 7 octets when routing over multiple hops. RFC 6282 updates RFC 4944 and makes the old HC1/HC2 format NOT RECOMMENDED for sending.

today: RFC 6282 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4944, and it is itself updated by RFC 8066. The RFC makes the RFC 4944 header compression NOT RECOMMENDED for new senders.

sections.title: Why RFC 4944 Compression Was Not Enough
sections.content:
The IEEE 802.15.4 standard specifies an MTU of 127 bytes, which leaves about 80 octets of MAC payload with security enabled, on a link of 250 kbps or less. RFC 4944 defined how to carry IPv6 over such links, including stateless header compression called LOWPAN_HC1 and LOWPAN_HC2.

RFC 6282 says these are insufficient for most practical uses. HC1 works best for link-local unicast, where both addresses can be elided entirely, but application traffic usually uses routable addresses. For those, HC1 needs the prefix in-line, needs 64 bits for the interface identifier even when it comes from a 16-bit short address, and needs the full 128-bit address for multicast.

So this document defines LOWPAN_IPHC for Unique Local, Global and multicast addresses, based on shared state called context. It also defines LOWPAN_NHC for arbitrary next headers.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of shortening messages only worked well for talking to neighbours. Most real messages go farther, so a better trick was needed.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 4944
sections.content:
This format is intended to replace the compression in Section 10 of RFC 4944. Implementing that old section is now NOT RECOMMENDED. New implementations MAY decompress it but SHOULD NOT send packets compressed that way. A compliant implementation MUST be able to process packets that use RFC 6282.

Fragmentation still works as in RFC 4944 Section 5.3: fragment sizes and offsets refer to the datagram before compression. As a result, any header that cannot fit within the first fragment MUST NOT be compressed.

The new dispatch values preempt the ESC dispatch value from RFC 4944. The value 01 000000 is reserved as a replacement for ESC.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rules replace the old shortening method. Devices must understand the new one, and should stop sending the old one.

sections.title: The LOWPAN_IPHC Encoding
sections.content:
LOWPAN_IPHC assumes the common case: Version is 6, Traffic Class and Flow Label are zero, the Payload Length can be inferred from lower layers, the Hop Limit is a well-known value, and addresses are formed from the link-local prefix or a few routable prefixes with an interface identifier (IID) derived from the 802.15.4 address. The encoding uses 13 bits, 5 of them from the dispatch type, and begins with the bits 011.

The base format is two octets with these fields: TF (Traffic Class and Flow Label), NH (Next Header), HLIM (Hop Limit), CID (Context Identifier extension), SAC and SAM (source address compression and mode), M (multicast) and DAC and DAM (destination address compression and mode). Fields that are not fully elided follow the encoding in their original IPv6 order.

HLIM can be 00 (carried in-line), or 01, 10, 11 meaning a hop limit of 1, 64 or 255. The NH bit set to 1 means the next header is encoded with LOWPAN_NHC. The Version field is always elided, and the Payload Length MUST always be elided.

In the best case, a link-local packet needs only two octets (dispatch and encoding). When routing over multiple hops it takes 7 octets: 1 dispatch, 1 IPHC, 1 Hop Limit, 2 source address and 2 destination address. The Hop Limit cannot be compressed there because it is decremented at each hop.
sections.plainLanguage: Two small bytes act like a set of checkboxes that say which parts of the long header were left out and how to put them back.

sections.title: Compressing Addresses and Context
sections.content:
For unicast with SAC=0 (stateless), SAM selects how much of the address is carried: 00 all 128 bits, 01 the last 64 bits with the link-local prefix elided, 10 16 bits (the IID is 0000:00ff:fe00:XXXX), and 11 nothing, with the IID computed from the encapsulating header. With SAC=1 the address is built from context, a prefix shared between compressor and decompressor. In that mode SAM 00 means the unspecified address ::.

How contexts are shared and maintained, what they contain, and what to do with unknown or invalid contexts are all out of scope. Up to 16 contexts can be used. When CID is 1, an extra octet carries a 4-bit Source Context Identifier (SCI) and 4-bit Destination Context Identifier (DCI). Context 0 is the default.

When the IID is elided, it comes from the 802.15.4 address. An extended address (EUI-64) is turned into an IID as in RFC 4291 Appendix A by inverting the universal/local bit. A 16-bit short address is mapped by setting the middle 16 bits to 0xfffe, the bottom 16 bits to the short address and everything else to zero. Bits may be elided only if they match this mapping and MUST NOT be elided if they do not.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone in the neighbourhood already knows the street name, you can write only the house number. The shared list of street names is the context.

sections.title: Traffic Class, Flow Label and Multicast
sections.content:
The 8-bit Traffic Class is split into 2-bit ECN and 6-bit DSCP. The TF field says what is carried: 00 ECN, DSCP, 4-bit pad and Flow Label (4 bytes); 01 ECN, 2-bit pad and Flow Label (3 bytes); 10 ECN and DSCP (1 byte); 11 everything elided. The Traffic Class is rotated right by 2 bits so the ECN bits always sit in the same place.

Multicast addresses (M=1) with DAC=0 can be compressed to 48, 32 or 8 bits (DAM 01, 10, 11), taking the forms ffXX::00XX:XXXX:XXXX, ffXX::00XX:XXXX and ff02::00XX. This covers the Solicited-Node Multicast Address and any multicast address whose upper group identifier bits are zero.

With DAC=1, DAM 00 compresses Unicast-Prefix-based multicast addresses (RFC 3306 and RFC 3956) down to 6 octets, taking the prefix from context. The other DAM values are reserved.
sections.plainLanguage: Some labels on a message are usually blank, so they are skipped. Group addresses, used for talking to many devices at once, also get short forms.

sections.title: Next Header Compression and UDP
sections.content:
When NH is 1, the bits right after the compressed IPv6 header start a LOWPAN_NHC encoding. Headers encoded this way must be contiguous, each preceded by an IPHC or NHC encoding. Extension headers get an octet 1110 EID NH: EID 0 is Hop-by-Hop Options, 1 Routing, 2 Fragment, 3 Destination Options, 4 Mobility and 7 an IPv6 header (EIDs 5 and 6 are reserved). Their Length field counts octets rather than 8-octet units, so such an extension header can have at most 255 octets after the Length field, and a trailing Pad1 or PadN may be elided.

UDP uses the octet 11110CPP. The C bit set to 1 elides the 16-bit checksum. The P bits choose ports: 00 both 16-bit ports in-line, 01 destination port is 0xf0 plus 8 bits, 10 source port is 0xf0 plus 8 bits, 11 both ports are 0xf0b plus 4 bits. The UDP Length field MUST always be elided.

Because ports 0xf0b0 to 0xf0bf tell little about the application, the RFC recommends using them with a mechanism such as a TLS Message Integrity Check, and suggests stacks avoid using them as dynamic ports.
sections.plainLanguage: Headers that come after the main one can be shrunk too. UDP port numbers that start the same way are written as just the last few digits.

sections.title: Eliding the UDP Checksum Safely
sections.content:
The UDP checksum is mandatory with IPv6, so RFC 4944 disallowed compressing it. Here a compressor MAY elide it only with upper-layer authorization, and MUST NOT set the C bit without it. The upper layer may authorize only for tunneling (where the tunneled data has its own addressing, security and integrity check) or when a message integrity check such as the IPsec Authentication Header covers at least the same information with at least the same strength.

In addition, a link-layer integrity check MUST be used on frames carrying such packets, since otherwise a packet could be delivered to the wrong destination. The compressor MUST verify the checksum before eliding it, and drop the packet if that fails. The decompressor MUST recompute the checksum, MUST verify the integrity check, and MUST drop the packet if it cannot unambiguously determine that the check exists or if verification fails.

A forwarding node MAY infer authorization only if it can unambiguously determine and verify an integrity check covering the same data. Otherwise it MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: Skipping the checksum is like skipping a seal on a package. It is only allowed when something else is already guaranteeing the package arrives intact.
